newsitem.title: FRANCE: French press hails battling Chirac in Israel.
newsitem.headline: French press hails battling Chirac in Israel.

text.p: French newspapers hailed President Jacques Chirac on Wednesday for confronting zealous Israeli police in Jerusalem's Arab quarter, but said his anger was not as spontaneous as it looked and could backfire.
"Battling Jacques", the daily France-Soir exclaimed in a banner headline in English, likening Chirac to Lucky Luke, the daring lonesome sharpshooter cowboy of a popular French cartoon.

Other commentators said his tough-guy attitude during his tour of Israel recalled that of his presidential mentor Charles de Gaulle. But they said Israel might now portray France as too pro-Arab to play a role in Middle East peace.

All main newspapers carried frontpage pictures of Chirac, red-faced with anger, as he forced his way on Tuesday through Israeli bodyguards and police to demand they leave him in peace to greet Palestinians and visit Christian, Moslem and Jewish holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem.
"Facing the soldiers, Jacques Chirac imposed himself by his physical presence even more than by the prestige of his job," the pro-government Le Figaro said.
France-Soir praised the presidential anger in the face of tight security which it described as a trap set up by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
But Chirac also displayed "staggering boldness or a lack of awareness", as if he had hoped to plunge into the crowd in the tense city as he does when touring French villages, it said.

Netanyahu has apologised for what he called "perhaps excessive zeal in trying to protect a friend", explaining that VIP security had become an obsession since the assassination of prime minister Yitzhak Rabin nearly a year ago by an extreme-right Jew.
Chirac later said he regarded the incident as closed.
"Was our president hoping to turn all by himself the Holy City into a city open to all religions?" France-Soir asked.

"(Chirac) paid back the Israelis," the Gaullist Le Figaro said. It said Chirac used the occasion to retaliate after Israel banned French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette from visiting the headquarters of the Palestine Liberation Organisation in Jerusalem.

"Chirac knows full well that a picture is worth 1,000 speeches. The presidential anger was highly symbolic," it said, adding the episode was intended to tell the Arab world that France did not recognise Israeli sovereignty on East Jerusalem.

But several commentators voiced scepticism about whether Chirac would benefit from the confrontation, which dramatised Franco-Israeli differences over the terms for Middle East peace, the role of Europe and the status of Jerusalem.
Le Figaro said the Jerusalem incident would prompt hardline Netanyahu to make Chirac's task even more difficult as he tries to regain a major role for France and Europe in the Middle East.
"The Israeli premier will seek to push France into having nothing more than an Arab policy," it said.
The left-wing daily Liberation said Chirac had been inspired by de Gaulle. But unlike Chirac, de Gaulle was not claiming to act on behalf of Europe.
"(Chirac) risks giving arguments to those who suspect that he is only seeking to have Europe endorse French policy under the pretext of a common foreign and security policy," it said.
